transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Solutions), Maya Thompson (Head of ML, Aurora), Daniel Kim (Platform Eng, Aurora), Sofia Perez (CTO, Aurora)
---
00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off in a minute, uh we're doing a ~45 minute walkthrough of Optimize focusing on batching and the prefix / KV cache cost model.
00:12 Maya: yep, thanks. we have about an hour blocked. our main question is: can you get our per-transaction cost down while keeping p95 < 200ms for scoring and context lookups?
00:26 Jordan: totally. quick intros — i'm jordan, i'm the AE, priya here will run through the technical pieces. priya, want to take it away?
00:33 Priya: yeah thanks. so i'll frame this as three parts: 1) batching basics, 2) prefix vs KV cache recommendations for your retrieval use case, 3) cost model and example numbers. i'll call out where dedicated vs hosted changes the numbers.
00:48 Priya: quick note — transcription might show KV as K-V or K V, so apologies for any typos.
01:05 Priya: (slides share) first, batching. we look at two axes: tokens per request distribution and inter-arrival time. for Aurora you told us earlier you have a mix: short scoring requests (50-150 tokens) and long context assembly calls (400-1k tokens). that mixes badly for naive batching.
01:22 Daniel: yeah correct. most realtime scoring is <200 tokens, but we also do customer summary generation that pulls a 2-3k context but can be async.
01:34 Priya: perfect. for short requests we recommend tight latency buckets and small batch sizes (batch window ~5-10ms) to preserve p95; for the longer async jobs, allow larger batch windows to increase throughput. Redwood Optimize will suggest these buckets automatically after sampling your traces.
01:50 Maya: can you quantify cost impact? Like what does batching give us in dollars or tokens?
01:56 Priya: yes — rough example: on a gpus pool similar to the one you run, grouping short requests into 8-16 request batches can reduce per-token overhead by ~10-20%, and for long-context batching we see up to 30-40% improvement due to KV cache reuse across concurrent sessions. those are estimates; we will run the pilot against your traces to give concrete numbers.
02:20 Jordan: also, there's a tradeoff — bigger batch windows can add latency tail. we tune for p95 targets.
03:00 Priya: moving to prefix vs KV cache. Prefix cache is basically caching token prefixes that are identical across many calls — low memory footprint, good when you have repeated templates/prompts. KV cache stores the model's keys/values for past tokens to avoid recomputing attention for long contexts — higher memory but massive compute savings on long sequences.
03:18 Priya: in your case, since you do a lot of retrieval augmented generation (RAG) like lookups + short scoring, KV cache is valuable when the same context is requested repeatedly (e.g., frequent customer history reads). prefix cache helps with system prompts and fixed templates.
03:32 Maya: we have repeated reads of the last 500 tokens for account history. would that map to KV cache?
03:38 Priya: yes, that's a classic KV use. hit rates depend on how many distinct users and session fragmentation. if you have sticky routing (per-user slot) hit rates go way up.
03:46 Daniel: we're on GKE with our services in a single region; session affinity is doable via our load balancer. any red flags for running KV cache in hosted vs dedicated?
03:54 Priya: good question. hosted can do caching but we recommend Redwood Dedicated for predictable memory footprint and guaranteed slot isolation when you need sustained high KV capacities. hosted will fallback gracefully to cheaper variants but for tight p95 you might prefer Dedicated.
04:12 Jordan: for cost modeling we usually show both hosted unit cost and dedicated break-even points.
05:00 Priya: here's an example cost table — (we reference a shared sheet link) assume 100k daily requests, 70% short scoring, 30% long-context. the model uses three levers: batching factor, KV cache hit rate, and quantization profile. with batching factor 10 and KV hit 60% we estimate X cost per 1M tokens vs baseline.
05:25 Maya: can you share the sheet? we couldn't open it before the call.
05:28 Jordan: yes putting link in chat now — redwood.com/sheets/optimize-pilot-aurora (note: placeholder).
06:00 Priya: some gotchas: KV cache memory grows with sequence length. if you store full 2k kv per session and have 10k concurrent sessions, memory goes up fast. so we recommend TTL + eviction + sticky assignment.
06:18 Sofia: (laughs) i spelled my name wrong earlier in the calendar, so you have sofia with an f.
06:23 Jordan: got it, thanks sofia.
06:28 Priya: security — we support KMS integrations for key material and bring-your-own-keys on Dedicated/Private. SOC2 is in place for hosted plane; for Private deployments we can work with your security team for air-gapped installs.
06:55 Daniel: do you log request payloads centrally? we need audit logs but not retain PII.
07:00 Priya: we have token-level cost and latency logs, and you can configure redaction. for Dedicated you keep control over retention. i'll attach the security brief.
08:00 Priya: back to caching: the hit-rate math — if you increase KV hit-rate from 20% to 60% you offload a lot of compute; here's the intuition: KV hit avoids recomputing the attention for past tokens, so for long contexts it reduces per-request compute by up to 50-70% depending on model. that translates to lower GPU time and thus cost.
08:25 Maya: what are realistic hit rates for us? we have ~1M users, but top 10k users are very active.
08:35 Priya: with sticky routing and per-user slot caching, you could get 50-70% hit for the active cohort, and lower for tail. Optimize will give a distribution and recommended cache size.
08:47 Jordan: we also suggest hybrid: prefix cache for system prompts + small frequent prefixes, and KV for per-user histories. that captures quick wins without huge memory commitments.
09:30 Priya: demo time — i'll show the Optimize console. (screen: console) top-left is the recommended batching policy; you can set latency SLOs and cost weight. the profiler sampled traces and suggested 3 buckets: realtime (5-10ms window), interactive (20-50ms), async (200-500ms).
09:50 Priya: note the system automatically recommends quantization profiles per model; HQ quantization helps cost but affects quality slightly — we surfaced eval delta metrics.
10:10 Daniel: how do we evaluate quality regressions from quant? we can't afford customer-facing hallucinations.
10:16 Priya: we tie quality monitoring to prompt sets and evals. you can define key prompts for aurora (e.g., balance explanation) and we run regression alerts when quantized model diverges beyond thresholds.
10:30 Maya: good. also curious about failover — if a model variant fails, what's fallback?
10:36 Priya: we have model variants and automatic fallback policies. you can route between cost-optimized and accuracy-optimized models; fallback occurs automatically if latency or error thresholds breach.
11:10 Maya: is there a minimum commit for Dedicated? we have bursty months (end of quarter traffic).
11:16 Jordan: Dedicated typically has a monthly commit; we can architect burst capacity to be on-demand and cover spikes. we'll include example reserved vs burst plan in pricing.
12:00 Priya: random note — sometimes transcription shows "KV cache" as "kay vee cache" in logs, ignore.
12:30 Daniel: one technical detail: our GKE nodes have 256GB RAM; how many KV slots per GPU do you estimate?
12:38 Priya: depends on model and kv size. for a 2k sequence with float16 keys+values, estimate ~200MB per slot; you can put ~12 slots on a 32GB GPU with quantization; on larger GPUs it's more. we'll run exact mem calc in the pilot.
13:01 Priya: yes — we can tune TTL + LRU bucketization and recommend the size for target hit-rate.
14:00 Priya: (switch back to sheet) now talking pilot plan: we want sample traces, you allow us to run bench in a staging S3/GKE setup, we run 48 hour benchmark capturing latency, cost, and hit rates. then we deliver a summarized sheet with recommended batching policy and cache sizing.
14:20 Daniel: how do we supply traces? do you need raw payloads?
14:26 Priya: ideally anonymized request/response traces including token counts and inter-arrival times. you can sanitize PII and keep identifiers hashed. we only need distribution shapes.
14:36 Maya: our legal team will ask about retention. how long do you keep traces?
14:40 Jordan: for the pilot we keep traces for 30 days, but we can tighten that in the agreement.
14:46 Priya: one more piece — routing policy: if you want higher hit rates, use sticky routing by user ID to keep sessions on the same slot. this requires load balancer affinity; good to know you can do sticky.
15:15 Daniel: yep we can.
16:03 Jordan: we'll do initial sampling within 3 business days, then a 48-hour benchmark scheduled at mutual availability, results within a week after the run. so roughly 10 business days end-to-end.
17:05 Sofia: p99 is less critical, we focus on p95 < 200ms for scoring, but p99 < 500ms would be nice.
18:18 Priya: two things: 1) over-allocating KV for the whole user base instead of active cohort; 2) setting batch windows too large for realtime buckets and hurting tail latency. both are fixable and Optimize flags them.
18:32 Jordan: ok let's surface the proposed next steps: we'll send pricing and sample contract, attach security + KMS docs, priya will share the cost sheet and a checklist for traces, and we schedule the benchmark.
18:51 Maya: actionable. can you include example mem calc per GPU in the sheet?
18:55 Priya: yes i'll add memory calc and an example eviction config.
19:30 Daniel: small question — do you support model quantization that still retains 16-bit kv?
19:36 Priya: yes some quantization paths preserve kv precision; we recommend mixed precision for critical workloads. we'll note that in the sheet.
19:48 Sofia: on compliance: we'll need a remediated SOC2 report and details on access controls.
20:07 Jordan: understood, we'll include SOC2 report and list of RBAC and SSO options.
20:33 Jordan: final minute — recap of next steps. Jordan to send pricing and contract, Priya to share security + cost sheet + mem calc, Daniel to share anonymized traces, schedule benchmark early next week.
20:50 Maya: thanks everyone. good session.
21:00 Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up in chat with links and dates. bye.
